t.7.1.1: When Rāma had regained his kingdom and the slaying of the Rākṣasas had been accomplished, all the sages came to congratulate Rāghava.
t.7.1.2: Then came Kauśika, Yavakrīta, Raibhya, and Cyavana as well, and Kaṇva, the son of Medhātithi, those sages who dwelt in the eastern quarter.
t.7.1.4: Pṛṣadgu, Kavaṣa, Dhaumya, and the great sage Raudreya, those who had taken refuge in the western quarter, also came, accompanied by their disciples.
t.7.1.3: Svastyātreya, the blessed Namuci, and likewise Pramucu, all those who dwelt in the southern quarter, came together with Agastya and his followers.
t.7.1.5: Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and then Atri, Viśvāmitra, and then Gautama, Jamadagni and Bharadvāja: these too, the seven great seers, came.
t.7.1.6: Having reached the dwelling of Rāghava, these great-souled ones, radiant as fire, stood waiting for the doorkeeper to announce them.
t.7.1.7: Then, at the word of Agastya, the doorkeeper swiftly went in and quickly entered the presence of the great-souled Rāghava.
t.7.1.8: Seeing Rāma, whose radiance was like that of the full moon, he at once announced to him that Agastya had arrived together with the ṛṣis.
t.7.1.9: Hearing that those sages, radiant as the rising sun, had arrived, the king then said to the doorkeeper, "Show them in, as they please."
t.7.1.10: Seeing those sages arrived, Rāma rose to meet them with joined palms, and, having respectfully saluted them, self-composed, he directed that seats be offered to them.
t.7.1.11: Those bulls among sages sat down, each according to his rank, upon those seats adorned with gold, well spread with coverings and comfortable.
t.7.1.12: Asked by Rāma after their welfare, the great seers versed in the Vedas, together with their disciples and their leaders, spoke these words to Rāma.
t.7.1.13: O mighty-armed one, O Raghunandana, all is well with us everywhere; but by good fortune we see you well, your enemies slain.
t.7.1.14: That Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, was surely no burden for you, O Rāma, for bow in hand you could conquer the three worlds; of this there is no doubt.
t.7.1.15: Fortunately, O Rāma, Rāvaṇa along with his sons and grandsons has been slain by you; fortunately, today we behold you victorious, together with your wife.
t.7.1.16: By good fortune, Prahasta, Vikaṭa, Virūpākṣa, Mahodara and the invincible Akampana, those night-roamers, have been slain.
t.7.1.17: Kumbhakarṇa, whose size no greater size in this world surpasses, has by good fortune been struck down by you in battle, O Rāma.
t.7.1.18: By good fortune you entered into single combat with the lord of the Rākṣasas, who could not be slain by the gods, and you have won the victory.
t.7.1.19: The defeat of that Rāvaṇa in battle is nothing at all; but by good fortune Rāvaṇi, who had entered into single combat, was slain by you.
t.7.1.21: But this is our wonder, O gentle one, on hearing that Indrajit has been slain, he who was unslayable by all beings, the wielder of great illusion in battle.
t.7.1.20: By good fortune, O mighty-armed one, you have been freed from that enemy of the gods who rushed at you like Death itself, and victory, O hero, has been won by you.
t.7.1.22: O hero, having bestowed this holy and gentle gift of freedom from fear, by good fortune you prosper through victory, O Kākutstha, tormentor of enemies.
t.7.1.23: Having heard the words of those sages of purified souls, Rāma, filled with the greatest wonder, spoke with joined palms.
t.7.1.25: Passing over the rākṣasa Mahodara, Prahasta and Virūpākṣa, men of great valor, why do you praise the son of Rāvaṇa?
t.7.1.24: Why do you, passing over Kumbhakarṇa and the night-roamer Rāvaṇa, those two of great valor, praise Rāvaṇi?
t.7.1.26: Of what sort, indeed, is his power, what is his strength, what is his valor? Or by what reason does he surpass Rāvaṇa?
t.7.1.27: If it is fitting for me to hear, and I do not command you, and if it is not a secret too guarded to tell, I wish to hear it; let it be told: how was Śakra conquered by him, and how did he obtain his boon?
